title: No fraction fits
hook: With big enough numbers, surely some fraction hits √2 exactly?

knows: the diagonal of a 1-by-1 square is √2 (Pythagoras)
even and odd numbers; the idea of a proof by contradiction
doesNotKnow: why no fraction of whole numbers equals √2

misconception: With big enough whole numbers, some fraction will hit √2 exactly.
objective: The learner can explain that p/q = √2 would need p² = 2q², that 2q² keeps landing next to squares but never on one, and that the parity argument shows it never can.

claims.text: The diagonal of a 1-by-1 square is √2.
A fraction p/q equals √2 only if p² = 2 × q².
claims.source: Square both sides of p/q = √2 and multiply by q².

claims.text: 2 × 12² = 288 and 17² = 289, off by 1; the misses are exactly 1 at q = 1, 2, 5, 12, 29, 70, and for q from 1 to 70 the nearest square is never equal.
claims.source: Recomputed with node for q = 1..70 (and no q up to 100000 gives a perfect square). The miss-by-1 values are the Pell numbers (solutions of p² - 2q² = ±1). The stage computes every value it shows from the same function. Illustration only: a table cannot prove it.

claims.text: If √2 = p/q in lowest terms then p is even, so q is even too, a contradiction; so √2 is not a fraction of whole numbers (it is irrational).
claims.source: Classical parity proof, recorded in Aristotle, Prior Analytics I.23, and in later editions of Euclid's Elements (X, appendix); e.g. Hardy, A Mathematician's Apology, sec. 14.

recall.question: A friend says: 'My computer found p and q, each with a million digits, so that p/q is exactly √2.' What do you say?
options: Impossible: p² = 2q² would force p and q both even, forever
Possible, if the numbers are big enough
Possible, but only with a computer
recall.why: Exact equality needs p² = 2q². That makes p even, then q even, so the fraction can always be reduced: no lowest-terms fraction works, at any size.
